title: The Body as City: Sense-Storehouses, the Heart-King, and the Mind of Light at the Gates
arc: Beginning from the molding of Adam and Eve after the stolen icon of the Ambassador, the teaching traces how each sense became a storehouse-system serving the counsel of the heart-king, and ends with the Mind of Light arriving at the gates of this body-city to humble its archon-guards and seize the keys of all the senses.
reading:
The teaching opens with the cosmic backstory of the human body: Saklas and his companions, the archons that are Hyle, plotted to mold Adam and Eve. Lacking any image of their own that could rival the heavens, they took the imprint (the seal) of the icon of the Third Ambassador — the very likeness of the Exalted One they had glimpsed — and stamped it upon their molding. Sin, gushing forth from the archons (which is Hyle), ran upward, was cut off from the place above the firmaments, fell to the earth, and there molded the tree and its fruits. Through that operation in the fruits, the archons reached after the likeness of the Exalted One and fashioned Adam and Eve, each begetting "in his own kind, some in likeness, others not in likeness." The point of this opening is doctrinal: the human body is a counterfeit icon — a true seal pressed into a corrupt molding — and every member, every sense-organ, every interior chamber inside it is therefore an organ of the proprium that nevertheless carries the imprint of divine truth and can be reclaimed.

From this foundation the teaching turns to its main subject: the inner architecture of the body. The Molder placed in the molding of Adam and Eve members on the outside and on the inside — to each external sense-organ (an aisthēsis with its operation) corresponds an interior structure of houses, storehouses, granaries, caverns, and treasuries. Whatever the senses and elements take in from outside is carried inward and deposited there, kept against the time when the "demander" or "petitioner" returns to claim it. This is the doctrine of memory and recollection read correspondentially: the natural mind is built like a walled city of inner repositories, and each sense feeds its own quarter.

The teaching then walks through the senses one by one, treating each as a distinct enthumesis — a counsel-faculty with its own storehouses. The enthumesis of the eyes receives every likeness it sees, beautiful or bitter, of love or of hate or of desire, and carries it inward to its chambers. When the heart is drawn to look out again upon what it once saw, this enthumesis goes in, ponders, sits with the deposit, and brings it forth to whoever asks. The enthumesis of the ears does the same with every hearing, stores it, watches over it, and after long intervals (ten hundreds of days) brings the word back from the very place where it was first set. The enthumesis of the place of smelling matches the eyes and ears in pattern; so too the enthumesis of the mouth and tongue, in which the place of taste-receiving has its own caves and storehouses of stored tastes. The enthumesis of the touch of the hands holds every touch in its inner storehouse and produces the recollection on demand. Each sense, then, is not merely an opening but an entire interior household: gate, corridor, chamber, watcher, and stored deposit.

Above all these the heart is king. Whatever the five enthumeses gather inward they hand over as a deposit (a parathēkē) to the enthumesis of the heart, and she watches over them all. The teaching makes the political image explicit twice. First, the counsel of the heart is likened to a king before whom all the senators of the city and the principalities of his region lay matters; whenever his commanders come and request what they wish, he gives to them out of the senators and the gnome by which they walk. Second, he is likened to a cellarer (kellarites) who receives every item sent and arranges them in vessel by vessel, place by place, so that each can be retrieved from exactly where it was set. So the body-city is governed: senses gather, the heart-king deposits and adjudicates, and the whole interior is an ordered economy of stored impressions.

Having established the city, the teaching turns to its defenses. There are watchmen set upon the gates, nets stretched across the gateways, and guards holding the nets at the doors. The body itself is likened to an encampment with gates, towers, and watch-stations; its guards correspond to the gates and to the sense-organs of the body — the places of seeing, of hearing, of smelling, the speakers and the spoken words. A multitude of helpers is placed upon the members to assist them, and within all of this the enthumesis (which is the teaching of the body) is queen of the entire encampment: when she pleases, she opens; when she pleases, she shuts. A fellow-citizen, one reckoned to their own region, is admitted freely through the gate; the stranger is hindered, made to stand on his feet at the door, and not permitted to enter — or, if admitted, only with great toil, into many cells.

The whole long architectural description has been preparing for its decisive moment, which is the climax of the teaching. The Mind of Light comes to the gates of the body. The archons stationed at the gates — the same powers that descended from Hyle's molding and now hold the guard-stations of the senses — recognize him as a stranger and try to hinder him: "he is foreign to us, let him not enter." But the Mind of Light, in his wisdom, in his fear, and in his multitude, humbles those guards. When he has finished humbling them, he takes the keys out of the hands of all the gates of the body. Until that moment those gates had been opening only to the fantasy of desire — receiving inward the visions of pleasure, the meditations of the cares of the bios, the tastes of various defiled foods, and so feeding Sin within, who drew the whole heart after him. The Mind of Light's seizure of the keys reverses the whole economy: the archon-watchmen are dispossessed, the queen-enthumesis is no longer free to open and shut at the proprium's pleasure, and the storehouses that were filling with desire's deposits now come under the governance of illumined rational understanding.

The spiritual process being taught, then, is this. Because the body is built upon the stolen seal of the Ambassador, every sense-faculty is at once a corrupted gate of self-love and a potential receptacle of divine truth. In its unregenerate state the city is intact but inverted: the heart-king receives only what the senses gather from desire, and Sin draws the whole interior after him. Regeneration does not bypass this structure; it enters it. The Mind of Light comes precisely to the gates, contests the archons stationed there, humbles them, and takes the keys, so that thereafter what the senses gather, what the storehouses keep, and what the heart adjudicates may serve the Lord's truth instead of the proprium. The teaching is therefore a complete anatomy of how the natural mind is taken back: by recognizing that every sense is a storehouse with a guarded gate, every memory a deposit before the heart-king, and that the whole city changes hands when the Mind of Light masters its watchmen.

major_images.meaning: The will/love as governing center where all sense-deposits are handed over and arranged
